description: Field-DoS / griefing taxonomy modeling attacker-controlled COST ASYMMETRY: an attacker cheaply creates/fragments state (a tiny/dust/zero plot/deposit pushed to a victim's index set) so someone else's later required path (transfer/enumerate/claim/harvest/settlement) becomes expensive, reverting, or unusable. Drives griefing_dos_audit.py via griefing_dos_taxonomy.classify(). The class behind eval misses #379 (plot-spam transfer DoS), #485 (duplicate plotIndexes via sow), #491 (transferDeposit amount==0 recipient DoS).
_fp_note: NOT a flag-all-loops sweep. A loop is a signal only when bounded by USER-INPUT / STORAGE-LENGTH / EXTERNAL-ARRAY (a fixed small loop or a pure helper is not tagged). A storage write is a signal only when REPEATABLE-CHEAP or FRAGMENTING (.push / per-id entry), not a single balance update. Admin-only cleanup/config loops are not attacker-griefing unless the attacker influences the stored state. Pure/read-only loops are not high-risk unless on a transfer/claim/required path. HIGH-RISK requires attacker-controllable creation/growth AND a later-cost (consumer) signal — the asymmetry. Comments stripped before matching.

plot_spam.review_hint: Plots can be transferred/sown to a victim's plotIndexes set at low cost. If a later required path (transferPlots, enumeration, harvest) iterates plotIndexes, an attacker can spam many tiny plots to make the victim's path revert/OOG (#379).
examples: transferPlots iterating ids/starts/ends
sow pushing to plotIndexes

pod_fragmentation.review_hint: Pod/plot splitting or partial fills create many small fragments. Confirm fragmentation is bounded/charged and downstream enumeration isn't unbounded.
examples: partial fill creating a remainder plot each time

deposit_fragmentation.review_hint: Deposits can be transferred to a recipient's deposit-id list. Many dust deposits bloat the list and can make withdraw/enumeration expensive; pairs with zero_amount_edge (#491).
examples: transferDeposit adding a dust deposit to recipient list

token_id_fragmentation.review_hint: Many distinct token ids created cheaply can bloat per-account id enumeration.
examples: minting many fertilizer ids

storage_growth.review_hint: Appends to a per-account/global array that an attacker can grow cheaply. Confirm a cap or per-entry cost, and that consumers of the array are bounded.
examples: array.push(entry) reachable by attacker

unbounded_loop.review_hint: Loop bounded by an array/storage length that an attacker can grow. If on a required transfer/claim path, growth → OOG/revert DoS.
examples: for (i; i < account.plotIndexes.length; ++i)

user_controlled_loop.review_hint: Loop bounded by a caller-supplied array length. Confirm a sane cap; combined with per-iteration external calls or storage writes it is a gas/DoS surface.
examples: for (i; i < ids.length; ++i) over a calldata array

transfer_blocking.review_hint: A transfer path that iterates attacker-growable state can be blocked (revert/OOG) for the victim. The canonical #379 consumer side.
examples: transferPlots looping over the victim's plot set

recipient_revert_dos.review_hint: A recipient/user-controlled external call/hook on a required path can revert or consume gas to block progress (settlement/claim/transfer). NOTE: pure ERC1155/721 receiver DoS is owned by the token lens unless it touches field/plot/deposit state.
examples: push payment to a contract that reverts

approval_griefing.review_hint: Approval/allowance behavior usable to grief (front-run approve, allowance reset to block, operator self-grant). Confirm it cannot block a victim's legitimate flow.
examples: approval race blocking a transferFrom

zero_amount_edge.review_hint: Missing amount>0 check lets an attacker create zero/dust entries cheaply (a recipient-DoS / list-bloat primitive). #491: transferDeposit doesn't check amount==0 → recipient gets unbounded zero deposits. Tag when a create/transfer path lacks a positive-amount guard.
examples: transferDeposit with no require(amount > 0)

dust_rounding.review_hint: Rounding/partial-fill leaves dust remainders that accumulate as fragments. Confirm dust is swept or bounded.
examples: partial listing fill leaving a dust plot

array_bloat.review_hint: An unbounded per-account/global array grown by attacker actions. Confirm a cap and that all consumers are bounded; removal keeps the array compact.
examples: account.depositIdList / plotIndexes growth

mapping_bloat.review_hint: Per-key mapping entries created cheaply. Only a concern when something later iterates the keys (mappings aren't iterable in Solidity, so usually paired with an index array — check the array).
examples: nested mapping entry per attacker key with a parallel index array

batch_size_dos.review_hint: Batch op with no array-length cap. Usually self-DoS (caller pays) — only attacker-griefing if the batch iterates victim/shared state.
examples: batch transfer with no max length

gas_griefing.review_hint: External call inside a loop on a required path → a single griefing target can inflate gas / revert the whole operation.
examples: loop with an external transfer per element

state_cleanup_missing.review_hint: A create path with no matching cleanup/removal lets state grow monotonically. Confirm consumed/emptied entries are removed so the array/list does not bloat permanently.
examples: fully-withdrawn deposit not removed from depositIdList

claim_path_dos.review_hint: A claim/harvest/rinse path that iterates attacker-growable per-account state can be made too expensive to ever claim (funds locked).
examples: claimAll looping over a bloated deposit/plot set

lifecycle_lock.review_hint: A protocol-heartbeat / lifecycle step that iterates attacker-growable state — growth can brick the whole protocol (sunrise/settlement liveness).
examples: sunrise looping over a whitelist/well set an attacker can grow

low_cost_high_cost_asymmetry.review_hint: Generic cost-asymmetry: the same function both grows a per-account array AND loops over it (or a paired consumer does). Quantify create-cost vs later-path-cost and who pays.
examples: a function that pushes to and later iterates the same index array
